# Paths (data/, cache/, output_figs_appendix/) are relative to the REPOSITORY ROOT, not to
# this file's sub-folder; walk up to the folder holding the .Rproj file and knit from there.
find_repo_root <- function(path = getwd()) {
  p <- normalizePath(path)
  while (!length(list.files(p, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) {
    if (dirname(p) == p) stop("No .Rproj file found above ", path)
    p <- dirname(p)
  }
  p
}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = find_repo_root())
```

# Text for main manuscript
To account for the influence of seasonal salmon phenology on presence in the estuary (Kjelson et al. 1982; Munsch et al. 2020) we included f(WYdayij), a penalized thin-plate regression spline of water-year day (default basis dimension k = 10) whose effective flexibility was controlled by an estimated smoothing penalty rather than fixed a priori; cross-validation confirmed that catch inference was insensitive to the basis dimension for k = 3–10 and to standardization of water-year day (Appendix S#, Fig. S#)..

# Purpose of the seasonal smooth

Every catch model includes a smooth term, `s(water-year day)`, to absorb the within-season phenology of juvenile Chinook Salmon occurrence. Densities of
out-migrating parr rise and fall over the course of each season as a natural
consequence of growth, smolting, and emigration timing, independent of the
landscape covariates of interest. The smooth is therefore a nuisance /
adjustment term: its role is to remove this seasonal arc so that the
covariate effects are not confounded by sampling date, not to provide a
mechanistic description of migration timing. The intended shape is a smooth
seasonal arc rather than a highly flexible (over-fit) curve.

This appendix documents (i) how the smooth is constructed, and (ii) two
sensitivity analyses that confirm the specification is appropriate and that the
covariate inference is insensitive to reasonable alternatives.

# How the smooth is constructed

The models are fit with `brms`, which builds `s()` terms using the `mgcv`
penalized-regression-spline machinery. With no additional arguments,
`s(water-year day)` is a **thin-plate regression spline** (`bs = "tp"`), the
`mgcv` default. Two properties of this construction are central to the
sensitivity analyses below:

1. **The basis dimension `k` is an upper bound, not the realized flexibility.**
   The default `k = 10` yields `k - 1 = 9` basis functions after the
   sum-to-zero identifiability constraint (one unpenalized linear "null-space"
   term plus eight penalized "wiggly" coefficients).

2. **Smoothness is controlled by the penalty, not by `k`.** In the Bayesian
   formulation the eight penalized coefficients are treated as random effects
   with a single standard-deviation hyperparameter (`sds`), which acts as the
   smoothing parameter and is estimated from the data. Following standard
   practice (Wood 2017), `k` is set "large enough" and the penalty determines
   the effective degrees of freedom; a larger `k` does **not** by itself produce
   a wigglier fit, because the penalty shrinks unsupported flexibility toward a
   simpler curve. The weakly-informative default half-Student-\(t\) prior on
   `sds`, `student_t(3, 0, 2.5)`, was retained (see the priors appendix).

# Sensitivity analyses

Two questions were addressed empirically, using the backbone covariates common
to all catch models, `catch ~ outflow + s(water-year day) + offset(log(volume))`
with the same negative-binomial likelihood and the production sampler settings 
as used in the alernative fits described in main manuscript:
(4 chains, 3000 iterations, 2000 warmup, `max_treedepth = 12`,
`adapt_delta = 0.99`):

1. **Should the covariate be standardized before fitting?** The linear
   covariates are \(z\)-scored for interpretability and prior scaling. The
   smooth's input was left on its natural scale (water-year day). Because
   thin-plate splines are invariant to linear rescaling of the predictor, the
   fitted function should be unchanged by standardization; this was verified by
   refitting with a \(z\)-scored water-year day.

2. **Is the default `k` too permissive (does it over-fit)?** The model was
   refit across a range of basis dimensions (`k = 3, 4, 6, 10`). If the penalty
   is controlling smoothness as intended, the realized smooth and the
   out-of-sample predictive performance should be stable across `k`.

Models were compared by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO;
Vehtari et al. 2017). The data comprise
`r res$n` independent tows spanning water-year days
`r paste(range(round(res$smooths$x_raw)), collapse ="–")`,
with a sparse catch response
(`r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100*res$prop_zero)` zeros; maximum
`r res$max_catch`).

## Reproducible code

The full fitting and comparison code is shown below (not evaluated on render;
it is run once by `appendix_seasonal_smooth_sensitivity/appendix_spline_sensitivity.R`, which caches the
results loaded above).

```{r fit-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
library(brms)
d <- read_csv("data/tow_12_6_tps_nona.csv")
d$water_year_day_z <- as.numeric(scale(d$water_year_day))
priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "b"),
            prior(gamma(2, 0.1),  class = "shape"))

fit_k <- function(k, zscore = FALSE) {
  v    <- if (zscore) "water_year_day_z" else "water_year_day"
  kt   <- if (is.na(k)) "" else paste0(", k = ", k)
  form <- as.formula(
    sprintf("n_l_75 ~ out30_z + s(%s%s) + offset(log(Volume))", v, kt))
  brm(formula = form, family = negbinomial("log"), data = d, prior = priors,
      iter = 3000, warmup = 2000, chains = 4,
      control = list(max_treedepth = 12, adapt_delta = 0.99), seed = 1)
}

# k = 3, 4, 6, 10 (natural scale) + k = 10 on standardized water-year day
fits <- list(
  fit_k(10), fit_k(6), fit_k(4), fit_k(3), fit_k(10, zscore = TRUE))
loo_compare(lapply(fits, loo))
```

# Results

## Sampler and predictive diagnostics across specifications

```{r results-table}
tab <- res$stats %>%
  left_join(res$loo_compare %>% select(tag, elpd_diff, se_diff), by = "tag") %>%
  transmute(
    Specification   = tag,
    `k`             = k,
    `Std. input`    = ifelse(standardized, "yes", "no"),
    `sds (smooth SD)` = sprintf("%.2f", sds),
    `elpd_loo`      = sprintf("%.1f", elpd_loo),
    `Δelpd (SE)`    = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", elpd_diff, se_diff),
    `max Pareto-k`  = sprintf("%.2f", max_pareto_k),
    `Divergences`   = divergences)
kable(tab, align = "lccccccc",
      caption = "Table S1. Seasonal-smooth specifications. sds is the estimated
      standard deviation of the penalized spline coefficients (the realized
      smoothing parameter); Δelpd is the PSIS-LOO difference relative to the
      best-scoring specification (more negative = worse), with its standard
      error. All |Δelpd| are within ~2 SE of zero, i.e. statistically
      indistinguishable.")
```

Two patterns are clear:

- **Standardization has no effect.** The `k = 10` fit on natural-scale
  water-year day and the `k = 10` fit on standardized water-year day give an
  essentially identical smoothing parameter and predictive score
  (`sds` `r sprintf('%.2f', res$stats$sds[res$stats$tag=="k=10 (default)"])`
  vs `r sprintf('%.2f', res$stats$sds[res$stats$tag=="k=10 standardized"])`;
  `elpd_loo` differ by
  `r sprintf('%.2f', abs(res$stats$elpd_loo[res$stats$tag=="k=10 (default)"] - res$stats$elpd_loo[res$stats$tag=="k=10 standardized"]))`),
  confirming the expected scale-invariance of the thin-plate spline. The smooth
  was therefore fit on the natural water-year-day scale.

- **The result is insensitive to `k`.** Reducing `k` from 10 to 3 leaves the
  predictive score unchanged (all `Δelpd` within ~2 SE of zero; Table S1) and
  leaves the fitted curve visually unchanged (Fig. S1). As `k` decreases the
  estimated `sds` increases
  (`r sprintf('%.2f', res$stats$sds[res$stats$tag=="k=10 (default)"])` at
  `k = 10` to
  `r sprintf('%.2f', res$stats$sds[res$stats$tag=="k=3"])` at `k = 3`), i.e. the
  penalty compensates for the smaller basis so that the realized function is
  preserved — the signature of a penalty-controlled (rather than
  `k`-controlled) smooth. The most restrictive setting (`k = 3`) was the only
  one to show a sampling issue (a single divergent transition), indicating that
  over-restricting the basis is the greater practical risk.

```{r fig-s1, fig.cap="Figure S1. Partial effect of the seasonal smooth s(water-year day) (centered, log scale; shaded band = 95% credible interval) estimated at basis dimensions k = 10, 6, 4, 3 and at k = 10 on standardized water-year day. The fitted arc is a gentle, non-wiggly curve that is essentially identical across all specifications, confirming that the penalty — not k — governs smoothness.", out.width="100%"}
include_graphics(file.path(find_repo_root(), "output_figs_appendix", "appendix_spline_k_comparison.png"),
                 rel_path = FALSE)   # absolute path: knitting from this sub-folder
```

Conditional on outflow, the seasonal smooth is a shallow, single-arc adjustment:
much of the raw seasonal rise-and-fall in catch is already captured by the
outflow covariate, leaving only a modest residual seasonal term. There is no
indication of over-fitting at the default `k`.

# Conclusion

The default thin-plate specification is appropriate and robust:

- **Basis:** thin-plate regression spline, default basis dimension `k = 10`,
  fit on the natural water-year-day scale.
- **Smoothness:** governed by the estimated penalty (`sds`) under the default
  weakly-informative prior, not fixed a priori.
- **Robustness:** covariate inference and predictive performance are unchanged
  for `k` from 3 to 10 and are invariant to standardization of the smooth's
  input; the same specification is applied to every catch model so that the
  seasonal adjustment is consistent across the model set.

## Suggested methods / results sentence

> Season was modeled as a thin-plate regression spline of water-year day
> (`mgcv` default basis dimension *k* = 10) whose effective flexibility was
> controlled by an estimated smoothing penalty rather than fixed a priori;
> cross-validation confirmed that catch inference was insensitive to the basis
> dimension (indistinguishable PSIS-LOO for *k* = 3–10) and to standardization
> of water-year day (Appendix S#, Fig. S1).
